lessonTitle: Liver Disease: Jaundice, Cirrhosis, Portal Hypertension and Hepatic Encephalopathy

blocks.text: A 60-year-old man with a 25-year history of heavy drinking is brought in by his wife because he has become drowsy and muddled, and sleeps by day and wanders at night. His abdomen is swollen with fluid, his skin and eyes are yellow, and last week he vomited a cupful of blood. One failing organ explains the jaundice, the ascites, the bleeding and the confusion.

blocks.markdown: The liver receives about 75% of its blood from the portal vein, which carries nutrient-rich blood from the gut, and the rest from the hepatic artery. It synthesises albumin and clotting factors, detoxifies drugs and ammonia, makes bile, and **conjugates bilirubin**. Haem from red cells is converted to **unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin**, which is lipid soluble and travels bound to albumin. Hepatocytes conjugate it with glucuronic acid to make **conjugated (direct) bilirubin**, which is water soluble and excreted in bile; gut bacteria convert it to urobilinogen, some of which is reabsorbed and excreted in urine.

### Classification of jaundice

**Jaundice** is yellow discolouration of the skin and sclerae due to raised serum bilirubin (visible when it exceeds about 40 micromol/L). It is classified by the site of the defect: **pre-hepatic** (excess bilirubin production, as in haemolysis, overwhelming conjugation), **hepatic** (hepatocyte dysfunction, as in hepatitis or cirrhosis) and **post-hepatic** (obstruction of bile flow, as in gallstones in the common bile duct or pancreatic head cancer). Liver function tests (LFTs) separate them.

rows: Dark urine with bilirubin; urobilinogen absent
Gallstone obstruction, cancer of pancreatic head
blocks.caption: Jaundice classified by liver function tests (patterns, not exact thresholds)

blocks.title: Interpreting liver function tests
blocks.prompt: A patient has total bilirubin 150 micromol/L (80% conjugated), ALP 620 U/L (reference up to about 130), ALT 70 U/L, pale stools and dark urine. Classify the jaundice.

steps.text: A predominantly conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia means the liver is conjugating normally but bile cannot leave.
ALP is markedly raised relative to ALT, a cholestatic pattern from biliary epithelial induction, whereas ALT is only mildly raised.
Pale stools (no bile pigment reaching the gut) and dark urine (conjugated bilirubin excreted in urine) support obstruction.

blocks.answer: Post-hepatic (obstructive) jaundice, for example from a gallstone in the common bile duct or a pancreatic head tumour.

blocks.markdown:
### Cirrhosis and portal hypertension

**Cirrhosis** is diffuse hepatic fibrosis with replacement of normal architecture by **regenerative nodules**, the end stage of chronic liver injury. Stellate cells activated by chronic injury lay down collagen. The commonest causes are **alcohol-related liver disease, chronic hepatitis B and C, and metabolic dysfunction-associated (non-alcoholic) fatty liver disease**; others include autoimmune hepatitis, primary biliary cholangitis, haemochromatosis and Wilson disease. Distorted architecture and fibrosis raise resistance to portal flow, causing **portal hypertension**. Blood then diverts through **portosystemic collaterals** (oesophageal and gastric varices, rectal veins, and the umbilical region as caput medusae), bypassing the liver.

blocks.title: Portal hypertension
blocks.text: Portal hypertension is a sustained rise in pressure in the portal venous system, caused by increased resistance to flow. Causes are pre-hepatic (portal vein thrombosis), hepatic (cirrhosis, the commonest cause in developed countries) and post-hepatic (hepatic vein thrombosis, right heart failure). Its consequences are varices, ascites and splenomegaly.

items: Oesophageal varices: dilated submucosal veins at the lower oesophagus that can bleed catastrophically.
Ascites: portal hypertension, splanchnic vasodilatation and low albumin drive sodium and water retention and fluid transudation into the peritoneum.
Failure of synthesis: low albumin, prolonged prothrombin time from reduced clotting factors.
Hepatic encephalopathy, hepatorenal syndrome, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis and hepatocellular carcinoma.

blocks.caption: Serum-ascites albumin gradient (g/L). A value of 11 g/L (1.1 g/dL) or more indicates ascites caused by portal hypertension.

blocks.title: Determining the cause of ascites
blocks.prompt: Serum albumin is 30 g/L and ascitic fluid albumin is 22 g/L. Is portal hypertension the cause?

steps.text: The threshold is 11 g/L, and 8 is below it, so the gradient is low.
A low SAAG indicates ascites not caused by portal hypertension, such as peritoneal malignancy, tuberculous peritonitis or nephrotic syndrome.

blocks.answer: No. The SAAG is 8 g/L (low), so portal hypertension is unlikely to be the cause.

blocks.markdown:
### Hepatic encephalopathy

**Hepatic encephalopathy** is a reversible neuropsychiatric syndrome of liver failure, ranging from sleep reversal and confusion to coma, with a flapping tremor (asterixis). Ammonia is produced by gut bacteria from protein and by glutamine metabolism in the gut. Normally the liver converts it to urea. In cirrhosis, damaged hepatocytes cannot clear ammonia and **portosystemic shunting** lets gut-derived ammonia bypass the liver. Ammonia crosses the blood-brain barrier, and astrocytes detoxify it into **glutamine**, which accumulates, causing astrocyte swelling, cerebral oedema and altered neurotransmission. Precipitants include gastrointestinal bleeding (a protein load), infection, constipation, dehydration, hypokalaemia, diuretics and sedatives. Treatment addresses precipitants and lowers gut ammonia, for example with lactulose (an osmotic laxative that acidifies the colon and traps ammonia as ammonium) and the non-absorbed antibiotic rifaximin.

blocks.title: One process, many consequences
blocks.text: Cirrhosis causes both failure of hepatic function (jaundice, low albumin, coagulopathy, encephalopathy) and portal hypertension (varices, ascites, splenomegaly). Separate them mentally: function failure and pressure effects.

points: Jaundice is pre-hepatic (unconjugated bilirubin, normal ALP/ALT), hepatic (raised ALT with mixed bilirubin) or post-hepatic (conjugated bilirubin with markedly raised ALP, pale stools and dark urine).
Cirrhosis is fibrosis with regenerative nodules, caused mostly by alcohol, viral hepatitis and fatty liver disease, and leads to portal hypertension with varices, ascites and splenomegaly.
Hepatic encephalopathy follows failure to clear gut-derived ammonia, aided by portosystemic shunting, causing astrocyte glutamine accumulation and swelling.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old with sickle cell disease in a haemolytic crisis is jaundiced. His urine is a normal colour and his ALP and ALT are normal. Which bilirubin pattern is expected?

options.text: Raised unconjugated bilirubin, with no bilirubin in the urine
Raised conjugated bilirubin, with bilirubin in the urine
Raised conjugated bilirubin with markedly raised ALP
Normal bilirubin

questions.correctOptionText: Raised unconjugated bilirubin, with no bilirubin in the urine

distractorRationale.a: Correct: excess haem breakdown produces unconjugated bilirubin that is albumin-bound and not filtered, so urine is clear of bilirubin.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: conjugated bilirubin is water soluble and appears in urine, which suggests hepatic or obstructive disease.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: a cholestatic pattern with high ALP indicates obstruction.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: he is jaundiced, so bilirubin is raised.

questions.explanation: In haemolysis the liver is overwhelmed by bilirubin and the unconjugated fraction rises. Unconjugated bilirubin is bound to albumin and cannot be excreted by the kidney, so the urine is normal in colour (acholuric jaundice).

questions.stem: A 66-year-old woman has painless jaundice, itching, pale stools and dark urine. Her ALP is 8 times the upper limit and ALT is mildly raised. What is the likely level of the lesion?

options.text: Post-hepatic obstruction of the bile ducts
Pre-hepatic haemolysis
Acute hepatocellular necrosis
Gilbert syndrome

questions.correctOptionText: Post-hepatic obstruction of the bile ducts

distractorRationale.a: Correct: cholestasis with pale stools, dark urine and a high ALP indicates biliary obstruction.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: haemolysis gives unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with normal ALP.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: hepatocellular necrosis gives a markedly raised ALT.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: Gilbert syndrome causes mild unconjugated jaundice with normal liver enzymes.

questions.explanation: Conjugated bilirubin cannot reach the gut, so stools lose their pigment, and it regurgitates into blood and is excreted in urine. Bile duct cells upregulate ALP, which rises disproportionately to ALT in obstruction.

options.text: Diffuse fibrosis with regenerative nodules and distorted liver architecture
Acute hepatocyte swelling with reversible fat accumulation
A single focal mass of hepatocytes
Dilated bile ducts caused by gallstones

questions.correctOptionText: Diffuse fibrosis with regenerative nodules and distorted liver architecture

distractorRationale.a: Correct: fibrosis and regenerative nodules are the defining features.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: this describes steatosis, which is reversible and not cirrhosis.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: a focal mass suggests a tumour or adenoma.

questions.explanation: Cirrhosis is the end stage of chronic liver injury in which normal architecture is replaced by fibrous bands and regenerative nodules. The distorted architecture raises portal resistance and impairs function.

questions.stem: In a patient with cirrhosis and portal hypertension, why do oesophageal varices develop?

options.text: Portal blood is diverted through collateral veins connecting the portal and systemic circulations at the lower oesophagus
Low albumin dilates the oesophageal arteries
Coagulation factors accumulate in the oesophageal veins
Gastric acid damages the oesophageal veins directly

questions.correctOptionText: Portal blood is diverted through collateral veins connecting the portal and systemic circulations at the lower oesophagus

distractorRationale.a: Correct: raised portal pressure opens portosystemic anastomoses, and the thin-walled veins at the lower oesophagus dilate.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: low albumin contributes to ascites, not varices.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: clotting factors are reduced in cirrhosis, not accumulated.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: acid reflux does not create varices.

questions.explanation: When resistance in the liver is high, portal blood finds alternative routes to the systemic veins. The lower oesophageal anastomosis between the left gastric (portal) and oesophageal (systemic) veins is one such route, and the dilated submucosal veins may bleed.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains how hepatic encephalopathy develops in cirrhosis?

options.text: Gut-derived ammonia escapes hepatic clearance and shunting, and astrocytes convert it into swelling-inducing glutamine
High bilirubin directly damages cortical neurons
Excess urea synthesis causes cerebral hyperosmolarity
Low albumin leads to leakage of albumin into the cerebrospinal fluid

questions.correctOptionText: Gut-derived ammonia escapes hepatic clearance and shunting, and astrocytes convert it into swelling-inducing glutamine

distractorRationale.a: Correct: failed hepatic ammonia clearance plus portosystemic shunting raises brain ammonia, which astrocytes detoxify to glutamine, causing swelling.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: bilirubin neurotoxicity is a feature of kernicterus in neonates, not adult encephalopathy.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: urea synthesis falls in liver failure.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: this is not the mechanism.

questions.explanation: The failing liver cannot convert ammonia to urea, and portosystemic shunts let ammonia bypass the liver. In the brain, astrocytes combine ammonia with glutamate to form glutamine, and its osmotic effect causes astrocyte swelling and impaired neurotransmission.

questions.stem: A patient with ascites has a serum albumin of 31 g/L and an ascitic fluid albumin of 9 g/L. Calculate the serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) in g/L.
questions.explanation: SAAG = 31 - 9 = 22 g/L. A gradient of 11 g/L or more points to portal hypertension, such as cirrhosis, as the cause of the ascites.

questions.stem: A jaundiced patient has total bilirubin 120 micromol/L, of which 96 micromol/L is conjugated. What percentage of the total is conjugated?
questions.explanation: The conjugated fraction is 96 / 120 = 0.80, or 80%. A predominantly conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia indicates a hepatic or post-hepatic cause rather than haemolysis.

questions.stem: Describe how liver function tests and urine and stool findings differ between pre-hepatic, hepatic and post-hepatic jaundice.
markingGuide: Pre-hepatic: unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, normal ALT and ALP, no urinary bilirubin, increased urobilinogen
Hepatic: raised ALT/AST markedly, mixed bilirubin, dark urine
Post-hepatic: conjugated bilirubin, markedly raised ALP and GGT, pale stools, dark urine
Reason for pale stools: no bile pigment reaching the gut
Examples: haemolysis, hepatitis, gallstone or pancreatic head cancer
questions.explanation: The pattern follows where in the bilirubin pathway the problem lies. Enzymes distinguish hepatocellular from cholestatic injury, and the bilirubin fraction shows whether conjugation has occurred.

questions.stem: Describe the common causes of cirrhosis and explain how portal hypertension arises and what complications it produces.
markingGuide: Causes: alcohol, chronic hepatitis B and C, fatty liver disease, autoimmune and biliary disease, haemochromatosis, Wilson disease
Pathology: chronic injury, stellate cell activation, fibrosis, regenerative nodules
Distorted architecture increases resistance to portal flow
Portosystemic collaterals: oesophageal varices, caput medusae, rectal varices
Other complications: encephalopathy, coagulopathy, hepatorenal syndrome, SBP, hepatocellular carcinoma
questions.explanation: The fibrous, nodular liver impedes portal inflow, so pressure rises and collaterals open. The combination of raised portal pressure and falling synthetic function explains the full spectrum of complications.

questions.stem: A patient with cirrhosis becomes confused after a gastrointestinal bleed. Explain the mechanism of hepatic encephalopathy, why bleeding precipitates it, and the rationale for treating with lactulose.
markingGuide: Ammonia is produced from protein digestion and gut bacteria
Normal liver converts ammonia to urea; in cirrhosis hepatocyte function is reduced and portosystemic shunting bypasses the liver
Ammonia crosses the blood-brain barrier; astrocytes make glutamine, causing swelling and impaired neurotransmission
Blood in the gut is a protein load that raises ammonia production
Lactulose is an osmotic laxative that acidifies the colon, traps ammonia as ammonium and speeds its removal
Other precipitants: infection, constipation, sedatives, hypokalaemia
questions.explanation: Encephalopathy results from a rise in brain ammonia that the failing liver cannot clear. Bleeding adds a large nitrogen load to the gut, and lactulose lowers ammonia absorption by acidifying and clearing the colon.
